4483.cfw: The medieval Alanic texts carry no accent marks, and the three modern reconstructions of the older Ossetic accent disagree on its very type: Thordarson (2009) holds that Old Iranian free word stress survived and that the modern strong-vowel rule arose only after the 13th century, Kim (1999) reconstructs a Sogdian-like accent on the first strong vowel (otherwise the last syllable) already for Proto-Ossetic and rejects Thordarson's evidence, and Cheung (2002, restated in Cheung 2008 and Kambolov 2006) argues for fixed initial stress and rejects Kim's.

4492.prule: No positional rule. The 'accents' are three diacritics written word by word: circumflex = long vowel pronounced 'con alguna fuerça' (long + force, i.e. the stressed long vowel of Shaul's reading), breve = short syllable, diaeresis = doubled vowel. 4496.prule: Contrastive, lexically specified stress confined to a two-syllable window at the left edge of the word: primary stress falls on the first or the second syllable according to the lexical stress marking of the roots and affixes in the word (minimal pairs differ only in stress placement, e.g. (35) P3P-count 'to count them' vs VAL-count 'to count things'); the unmarked default position is the second (peninitial) syllable, and when lexical stress lies outside the window primary stress surfaces on the second syllable by default (p. 33). Vowel length is contrastive but plays no role in placement (quantity-insensitive).
4496.srule: Rhythmic: secondary stress on every other syllable after the primary stress -- on the 4th (6th...) syllable when primary stress is peninitial (the default), on the 3rd and 5th when primary stress is initial (lexically marked words); stress always alternates with neither clash nor lapse, and vowel length plays no role (left-to-right quantity-insensitive iambs). Established on words of at most five syllables (fn. 7); no lexical secondary stress assumed (fn. 9).

tn.translation: Samayé, like the great majority of Bantu languages, is a tone language. ... Samayé has three different tonal registers: a high register, written H; a mid register, written M; a low register, written B. ... The tone-bearing units are of two kinds: the vowels ... and the syllabic homorganic nasal consonant ... [p. 65] In view of this list one can conclude that there exist only two distinctive tones in Samayé, the tones /H/ and /B/ [L]. ... [p. 68] The low-falling tone will not figure in the tonological system of Samayé.

4502.prule: Fixed final: the basic word accent ('el acento básico de la palabra') always falls on the last syllable; preceding prefix syllables are in an unaccented position, where the prefix vowel a laxes to ä.

4502.tone: Full tone system: 'El chinanteco de Ozumacín puede tener tres, seis o nueve tonos, dependiendo del punto de vista desde el que se analice' (p. xi): three level tones (alto, medio, bajo), each also 'con acento' — ballistic accent, 'la elevación del tono disminuye rápidamente', written with a dot on the tone diacritic — plus three rising tones (p. xii), and tone sandhi across words and before pause ('Reglas morfofonémicas', p. xii). The ballistic 'acento' is a syllable-level property independent of the word stress of sec. 5.1: it occurs on prefixes too (e.g. preterite gaꜙ-, sec. 4.5.1), so it is not what 'siempre aparece en la última sílaba'. Verdict is fixed and quantity-insensitive, not tone or pitch accent, because the source does state a word-stress position; a reviewer may wish to flag that the stress statement is incidental and co-exists with a nine-tone system.

Los tres tonos básicos también se presentan con acento, en los cuales, la elevación del tono disminuye rápidamente. ... tn.translation: Ozumacín Chinantec can have three, six or nine tones, depending on the point of view from which it is analysed. ... There are three basic tones: high, mid and low. ... The three basic tones also occur with accent, in which the pitch height drops rapidly. ... One may think that the six signs presented so far represent six tones, or else that they are the same basic tones modified by the accent. ... In addition there are three tones that undergo a rise of the voice over the duration of the syllable.

4504.heavy: Three-way weight: light (CV), heavy (CVC, CVV), superheavy (CVVC, CVCC); superheavy syllables occur only word-finally; a stressed syllable must be long on the surface, so the short vowel of an open stressed penult is lengthened; final consonant treated as extrametrical (CVV<C>, CVC<C>). Shafi 2017 p. 76 also lists VC among heavy penults.
4504.dflt: Penult: an open light penult is made heavy by vowel lengthening and stressed (/so.ti/ -> [ˈsoː.ti] 'stick/cane'); light CV syllables never carry stress and a final non-superheavy syllable is not stressed (e.g. [ˈtʃaː.vəl] 'rice', 2024 [ˈʃæm.puː] 'shampoo').
4504.prule: Primary stress is confined to the last two syllables and is weight-driven: a word-final superheavy syllable (CVVC, CVCC; superheavies occur only word-finally) is stressed; otherwise the penult is stressed as a heavy syllable (CVV, CVC), and an open light penult has its short vowel lengthened so that it can bear stress (/so.ti/ -> [ˈsoː.ti]); light CV syllables are never stressed and stress never goes left of the penult. Metrical formalisation (p. 67): final-consonant extrametricality, moraic trochees built right-to-left non-iteratively, degenerate feet banned, End Rule Right. Shafi & Hellmuth 2024 (1): 'a) stress a final superheavy syllable, b) else the penultimate syllable'.
4504.srule: None: 'There does not appear to be any secondary stress in MP... we assume that only a single metrical foot is built in monomorphemic words' (Shafi 2017 §5.5 p. 76); restated by Shafi & Hellmuth 2024 §2.1: 'We have not found evidence in our data of secondary stress and thus assume that a single metrical foot is built per word.'

4508.dq: Phonological words, set off in this study by space, consist minimally of a single stressed syllable, and may have as many as four unstressed syllables preceding or following, or both. ... Analysis of phonological units larger than words has not yet been undertaken. (p. 14)

4508.prule: Exactly one stressed syllable per phonological word, and it is the tonic base (the stem): prefixes, proclitics and pretonic bases precede it unstressed (they carry tone), post-tonic bases follow it unstressed and toneless, so the stressed syllable is always the last toned syllable of the word, with up to four unstressed syllables on either side. Within a native bisyllabic base the stress is on its last syllable; Spanish loans keep their Spanish stress. The stress is of two lexically inherent types, ballistic vs controlled (a phonation contrast), which alternates by person/aspect in some verb bases.
4508.srule: None: one stressed syllable per phonological word (the tonic base); 'Pretonic syllables have tone but no stress; post-tonic syllables have neither tone nor stress.' The source's 'two stresses' are the ballistic vs controlled types of that single stress, not a secondary stress.

dfl.q: Most tonic bases are monosyllabic, and no native base longer than two syllables has been observed. A native bisyllabic base receives stress on its last syllable whereas a non-native polysyllabic base retains its foreign stress pattern. [p. 19] ... the stressed syllable is the last toned syllable of a phonological word [p. 14]

4509.quote: Sound Correspondences. General Yokuts i often > e in Paleuyami, e > i, and u > o, o > u. These shifts are most frequent in the stressed penult, sometimes involve the final syllable, but only occasionally the first syllable if there are three. When i and e, or again u and o, occur in the same word, there is thus an effect of vowel inversion by metathesis in Paleuyami. Frequent also is stressed a > e. [p. 232] ...
